# Digest of the #platform-oncall thread, Sunday 16 March 2025

sev3, 10:15 to 11:15 UTC. Summarised by role, oldest first. Runbook referred to: RB-025.

**10:31 support:** a partner integration reports TLS failures on about a third of its calls since around 10:15. Browsers show certificate warnings for some customers, not all.

**10:38 platform on-call:** request rate for edge-gateway-01 has been close to zero since 10:15 and the other two pods picked up the difference. The access logs show nothing wrong, as expected: a client that rejects our certificate never sends a request.

**10:45 platform on-call:** going through RB-025's list of certificate failures. Partial failure across many clients points at one pod rather than the clients' clocks.

**10:52 platform on-call:** `openssl s_client` with `-servername` against each pod. edge-gateway-01 presents a certificate whose notAfter is 2025-03-16 10:15 UTC. The other two present the renewed one. One pod missed the renewal.

**10:55 platform lead:** how? The certificate was renewed into the Secret on 2025-02-14, 30 days ahead. The renewal note at the time said to restart every edge pod, and whoever did it used `kubectl delete pod`, one at a time, waiting for each replacement to be Ready so two pods kept serving. They picked each name from a fresh pod list. The third time, the name at the top was the replacement created by the first delete, so that pod was restarted twice and the original pod behind edge-gateway-01 never was. Envoy reads the certificate only at start, so it kept the old one in memory for a month.

**10:56 platform lead:** and the daily outside probe kept reporting the new date, because it went through the load balancer and reached one of the renewed pods.

**10:58 platform on-call:** `rollout restart` on the edge-gateway Deployment. It brings up a replacement before retiring each old pod, so capacity never dropped below three.

**11:06 platform on-call:** every pod presents the renewed expiry date.

**11:15 platform on-call:** request rates look normal again on every pod. Closing.

**Agreed follow-ups:** renewals use `rollout restart`, never hand-deleted pods; after any renewal, check each pod with `s_client`, not just the public name; make the outside probe test each pod.
resolution: A rollout restart replaced all three edge pods; each now serves the renewed certificate.
root_cause: The February renewal was applied by deleting edge pods one at a time, and the original pod behind edge-gateway-01 was never deleted, so it still held the old certificate when that expired at 10:15.
symptoms: About one in three new TLS connections to the edge failed for an hour; request rates on edge-gateway-01 fell to almost nothing while the other pods carried more.
title: edge-gateway-01 kept serving an expired certificate

# Card processor pushed back for four minutes (sev4)

On 2025-06-02, between 22:05 and 22:10 UTC, the card processor turned away part of our traffic with its rate-limit response. card-processor-proxy-01 and card-processor-proxy-02 both logged `CPX-W429` from 22:05:20 to 22:09:10, and about 180 payments failed with `PAYAPI-E1107`. Customers saw a declined payment.

We were sending about 100 payment requests a second, a quarter of the 400 per second the processor allows our merchant account, so this was not our traffic hitting the limit. The processor reported a fault on its side. Nothing was changed on ours.

We have no runbook for the processor pushing back. If it happens again, write one.
resolution: The processor's side recovered on its own; no change on ours.
root_cause: A fault in the card processor's own rate counting rejected some of our requests although we were far under our limit.
symptoms: Both card-processor-proxy pods logged CPX-W429 and about 180 payments failed with PAYAPI-E1107.
title: Card processor pushed back for four minutes

# Refunds export starved the payments bouncers (sev2)

**When:** 2025-06-24, 13:20 to 14:05 UTC · **Owner:** team-payments · **Runbooks used:** RB-011, RB-010

## Summary

For 45 minutes on a Tuesday afternoon, card payments slowed down and a growing share of them failed with `503`. payments-api logged `PAYAPI-E1042` on all four pods. Nothing had crashed. A refunds export that finance ops had asked for was running inside payments-api itself, and its long transactions occupied the database connections that live payment traffic needed. The queue for those connections formed inside PgBouncer, on both instances at once.

## Impact

- `/v1/payments/*` latency started rising around 13:20. Failures followed within minutes and were worst around 13:40.
- A request that could not get a pool connection inside payments-api's 500 ms acquire deadline returned `503`. Customers saw a failed payment and could try again.
- Postgres itself had connections to spare throughout.

## How it looked at first

The page at 13:24 was on the `503` rate for payment routes. The pool panels told the familiar story from RB-010: 40 of 40 connections acquired on every pod, acquire wait p99 pinned at the deadline. RB-010 then asks what the database sessions are doing. They were `active`, not idle inside an open transaction, so the pods were not sitting on transactions while calling something else. They were waiting in line.

## Investigation

- 13:31 · `SHOW POOLS` on payments-pgbouncer-01 and payments-pgbouncer-02. Both the same: `sv_active` at 50 (40 regular plus 10 reserve), no idle server connections, `cl_waiting` near 30, `maxwait` near 4 s.
- 13:34 · `SHOW CLIENTS` counted about 80 payments-api clients per instance. An even split, so neither bouncer was carrying the other's share.
- 13:36 · the pgbouncer process on payments-pgbouncer-02 was far below a full core. The bouncer was not the bottleneck.
- 13:41 · on payments-db, `pg_stat_activity` grouped by statement: one statement held about 90 sessions with transactions averaging about 2 s. It was the export's.
- 13:44 · about 100 client backends out of 200 allowed by `max_connections`. The database had headroom; the wait lived entirely in the bouncers.

## Why the numbers fit together

Each of the four pods may hold 40 connections (`pool_max_conns=40`), so up to 160 client-side connections, roughly 80 landing on each bouncer. A bouncer opens at most 50 server connections. With all 50 busy, about 80 − 50 = 30 clients are left waiting, which is what `cl_waiting` showed. Two bouncers open at most 2 × 50 = 100 server connections, which matches the backend count.

Waits hovered around 4 s. That is past the 3 s after which the reserve pool opens, and well short of the 10 s after which PgBouncer disconnects a waiting client. So no client was dropped by the bouncer; every failure was payments-api giving up at its own deadline.

A transaction-pooled bouncer lends a server connection to a client for one transaction and takes it back at commit. Payment transactions last milliseconds. The export's took about 2 s each and were issued back to back from all four pods, enough to keep about 90 of the 100 server connections on the two bouncers occupied.

## Root cause

The export started at 13:10. It used the same pgx pool, the same database role and the same transaction-mode bouncers as live payments, and nothing capped how many export transactions could be in flight.

## Resolution

- 13:50 · export switched off.
- 13:51 · remaining export statements cancelled with `pg_cancel_backend`. `cl_waiting` dropped to 0 on both bouncers.
- 13:52 · `PAYAPI-E1042` stopped.
- 14:05 · resolved after 13 quiet minutes.

We followed RB-011 and did not raise `pool_max_conns` or `default_pool_size`: more clients would only have lengthened that queue.

## Follow-ups

1. Run exports outside the payment request path, with their own small pool. Owner: team-payments.
2. Alert when `cl_waiting` stays above 0 on either bouncer for a minute, so the page names the queue instead of the `503`s.
3. Exports that finance needs during the day get a size and concurrency review first.
resolution: The export was turned off and its remaining statements cancelled; the bouncer queues drained within a minute.
root_cause: A refunds export running inside payments-api held server connections for about 2 s per transaction and occupied about 90 of the 100 server connections on payments-pgbouncer-01 and payments-pgbouncer-02.
symptoms: Payment requests slowed, then failed with 503 and PAYAPI-E1042 on every payments-api pod while clients queued inside both PgBouncer instances.
title: Refunds export starved the payments bouncers

# The Sunday login flood

I was on call for team-identity on Sunday 3 August 2025. This is my account of a sev2 that ran from 10:10 to 10:45 UTC.

The page came at 10:14: the edge's `503` rate on `/v1/auth/login` was over its threshold. Other routes looked fine at first glance. The login graph didn't: attempts had gone from the usual 15 or so a second to about 150 a second at 10:08, and about 97% of them were failing on the password. They came from a wide spread of addresses. That pattern is credential stuffing, someone replaying leaked username and password pairs against us.

auth-service checks each password with bcrypt on the request goroutine. bcrypt is meant to be expensive, which is the point when someone steals the hashes and the problem when someone floods the login form. Each pod also caps itself: once 64 logins are in flight it answers `503` instead of queueing more, and the edge passed those straight through. The first ones went out at 10:10.

At 10:20 I worked through RB-002, because both pods were sitting exactly at their CPU limit. The throttling view showed about 70% of periods throttled, which on its own would send you looking for a thread count sized to the node. That wasn't it. Our Deployment sets `GOMAXPROCS` from the CPU limit, and it was 2 on both auth-service-01 and auth-service-02, matching the limit. This wasn't a mismatch making a half-idle pod stall; the pods really needed more CPU than the 2 they were allowed.

There is no rate limit on the login route at the edge; the only edge limit we have is on `/search`. So the quickest lever was the one RB-002 describes. At 10:27 I raised the CPU limit from 2 to 4 per pod and left the requests alone, so scheduling didn't change. The Deployment rolled one extra pod at a time with none taken away, and was done at 10:33. The `503`s stopped at 10:34, while the attempts were still arriving at the same rate. At 10:40 the attempts stopped as abruptly as they had started. I watched for five more minutes and closed it at 10:45.

What I'd like done:

1. A rate limit on `/v1/auth/login`, per client address and overall. It's not built, and nothing at the edge could have helped today.
2. An alert on the share of failed logins, which would have fired before the CPU did.
3. Keep the limit at 4 until the rate limit exists, then decide.
4. Accounts that saw a successful login during the run get a forced password reset. Security has the list.
resolution: The CPU limit was raised from 2 to 4 per pod; the 503s stopped at 10:34 and the attack ended at 10:40.
root_cause: A credential-stuffing run sent about 150 login attempts a second; each password check is CPU-heavy by design, so auth-service hit its 2-CPU limit and shed logins with 503 once 64 were in flight per pod.
symptoms: Logins returned 503 through the edge for about 24 minutes while login attempts ran at about ten times the normal rate.
title: Credential stuffing pinned auth-service's CPU

# redis-sessions failover on 12 November 2025: what happened

team-identity with team-platform. sev3. 18:05 to 18:15 UTC. We followed RB-018's checks during the incident.

**What did users see?**

From 18:05 some users were asked to log in again (`AUTH-E401X`). The sessions that were lost belong to logins handled by auth-service-02 between 18:05 and 18:07:45. A smaller group, whose sessions were created through the other auth-service instance in that window, also had a lookup fail when their next request went through auth-service-02; their sessions were not lost, and logging in again fixed it. By 18:09 `AUTH-E401X` was back to its usual trickle.

**Which node was the primary?**

redis-sessions-02, since the planned failover on 7 October 2025. redis-sessions-01 was patched after that one and stayed a replica. Since this incident redis-sessions-01 is the primary again.

**Why did Sentinel fail over?**

At 18:04:30 a host-firewall rule was added by hand on redis-sessions-02 during hardening work. It dropped traffic from the two VMs that run our other Sentinels, and nothing else: auth-service pods and the replication link from redis-sessions-01 still got through. Those two Sentinels stopped getting replies, waited out the 30 s `down-after-milliseconds`, agreed at 18:05:00 (2 of 3, our quorum), and promoted redis-sessions-01 at 18:05:05. Up to that moment replication was working, so nothing written before the failover was lost.

**Why were sessions lost after that?**

redis-sessions-02 never learned it had been replaced: the Sentinels that knew couldn't reach it. It still answered as a primary. The other auth-service instance switched to redis-sessions-01 at the failover; auth-service-02 kept its connections to redis-sessions-02 and went on writing sessions there. redis-sessions-01 had stopped replicating from it, so those writes existed only on the old node. The Redis Sentinel docs describe exactly this: writes accepted by an old master that clients can still reach are discarded when it rejoins as a replica.

**Where does `READONLY` come in?**

At 18:07:40 the rule was removed. The Sentinels reached redis-sessions-02 again and at 18:07:45 reconfigured it as a replica of redis-sessions-01, which drops its own data and copies the new primary's. auth-service-02 was still pointed at it, so its next session writes got `READONLY` until 18:07:49, when it moved to the new primary. That four-second window only works because the demoted node was reachable.

**How did we confirm it was over?**

At 18:09 Sentinel named redis-sessions-01 as master, and `INFO replication` on redis-sessions-02 showed it as a replica (`role:slave`). At 18:15 the replica's offset had caught up with the primary's, and we closed it.

**What changes?**

- Host-firewall changes on the Redis VMs go through config management with a review, never by hand (team-platform).
- team-platform will look at `min-replicas-to-write` for the sessions primary. The Sentinel docs describe it as the way to stop a primary that has lost its replicas from accepting writes.
- No change to auth-service. Completing the login when the session write fails is still the right call; it is why only the next request failed and not the login itself.
resolution: The firewall change was reverted, Sentinel turned redis-sessions-02 into a replica of redis-sessions-01, and auth-service-02 moved to the new primary.
root_cause: A hand-applied host-firewall change on redis-sessions-02 cut it off from the Sentinels on other VMs, which promoted redis-sessions-01 while auth-service-02 kept writing sessions to redis-sessions-02.
symptoms: From 18:05 auth-service logged a spike of AUTH-E401X; after the failover auth-service-02 briefly got READONLY from redis-sessions-02.
title: redis-sessions failover after a host-firewall change

# Handoff: night to day, 2025-11-18

**search-cluster-02, /var full. sev3, resolved. 05:30 to 06:40 UTC. Runbook: RB-008.**

Short version: one log file ate the root disk. Search was never affected because OpenSearch data lives on its own volume, `/data/opensearch`. What we lost is OpenSearch's own log lines on -02 between 05:30 and 06:10.

What I saw and did:

- 05:36 · paged by the "logs missing" alert for search-cluster-02. The only fresh lines were from the log agent itself, which ships its own errors over the network: `ENOSPC` writing its position file.
- 05:41 · `df -h /var`: 100% of the 40 GB root disk.
- 05:48 · `du -xh --max-depth=2 /var | sort -h`: one `*.log` file under `/var/log/opensearch/` at about 29 GB. Everything else normal.
- 05:52 · no OpenSearch entry in `/etc/logrotate.d/`. That's the RB-008 row for an unrotated app log, `/var/log/opensearch/*.log`.
- 06:02 · put the logrotate file back from config management (with `copytruncate`, because OpenSearch keeps the file open).
- 06:04 · `logrotate -f` on it. `/var` back to 11 GB, about 28%.
- 06:10 · OpenSearch lines arriving again.
- 06:40 · agent backlog shipped, nothing else growing. Closed.

Why it took this long to fill: -02 was rebuilt on 20 October 2025 and the rebuild never laid down the logrotate file. The log grows about 1 GB a day. From 20 October to 18 November is 29 days (11 left in October plus 18 in November), so about 29 GB of log on top of the usual 11 GB: 40 GB, the whole disk.

It wasn't silent. The `/var` warning at 90% (36 GB, so 25 GB of log, 25 days in) fired on 14 November around 05:30. That alert only opens a ticket, and nobody picked it up before the disk filled.

For day shift:

1. Config management: find out why rebuilt search-cluster nodes miss the OpenSearch logrotate file and check -01 and -03.
2. The 90% `/var` ticket needs an owner who reads it within a day.
3. If anyone needs OpenSearch logs from -02 for 05:30 to 06:10, there aren't any.
resolution: Restored the logrotate file from config management and forced a rotation; /var dropped to about 28%.
root_cause: search-cluster-02 was rebuilt on 2025-10-20 without its OpenSearch logrotate file, so one log under /var/log/opensearch/ grew about 1 GB a day until the 40 GB root disk was full.
symptoms: /var on search-cluster-02 reached 100%; OpenSearch stopped writing its log and the log agent reported ENOSPC, while search and indexing carried on.
title: search-cluster-02 /var filled by an unrotated OpenSearch log

# fraud-scorer-02 OOMKilled loop, 28 to 29 May 2026

sev4. UTC. Times after midnight are on 29 May. Runbook: RB-006.

```
21:52  node rotation drains the node under fraud-scorer-02; the replacement pod lands on one of the
       32-core nodes added to the general pool this month
22:00  pod Ready. WEB_CONCURRENCY is not set in the Deployment, so the entrypoint starts one gunicorn
       worker per CPU it can see: 32. The other pod, on a 16-core node, runs 16
22:11  first OOMKilled on fraud-scorer-02 (exit 137); kubelet restarts it
22:40  team-risk on-call starts on RB-006; kubectl top shows fraud-scorer-02 near its 3 GiB limit
22:48  redis-features --latency is normal and there are no feature-fetch latency warnings in the last
       hour. The cache growth RB-006 knows about needs a slow redis-features; not tonight
23:20  tracemalloc on one worker: allocations ordinary, nothing growing out of line
00:30  memory panel: fraud-scorer-02 climbs to the limit within minutes of each start; the other
       pod sits flat well below it
01:50  pgrep -P 1 on both pods: 32 worker PIDs on fraud-scorer-02, 16 on the other. Found it
02:30  WEB_CONCURRENCY=16 set in the Deployment; rollout
02:40  both pods running 16 workers
02:55  15 minutes without a kill; resolved
```

Between 22:11 and 02:30 the pod was killed about 20 times, once every 10 to 15 minutes.

## The arithmetic

A warmed-up worker holds about 150 MiB. Sixteen workers need 16 × 150 = 2,400 MiB, inside the 3,072 MiB (3 GiB) limit. Thirty-two need 4,800 MiB. The kill came once about 20 workers had warmed up (3,072 / 150 ≈ 20), which is why each start lasted about 11 minutes.

## Why RB-006 didn't point here

RB-006 is about memory growing inside each worker. Its stopgap, the `--max-requests` recycling, bounds how big one worker gets, not how many there are. Every check in it came back clean, which in the end was the clue: per-worker memory was normal, there were just twice as many workers.

## Follow-ups

- Keep `WEB_CONCURRENCY` set explicitly (now 16); never rely on the CPU-count fallback.
- Check the other Deployments whose worker or thread count comes from the visible CPU count, now that the pool mixes 16- and 32-core nodes.
resolution: WEB_CONCURRENCY=16 was set in the fraud-scorer Deployment and rolled out.
root_cause: WEB_CONCURRENCY was not set, so gunicorn started one worker per visible CPU; rescheduled onto a 32-core node, the pod ran 32 workers and needed more memory than its 3 GiB limit.
symptoms: fraud-scorer-02 was OOMKilled about 20 times overnight, each time within minutes of starting; the other pod carried the scoring traffic.
title: fraud-scorer-02 OOMKilled every few minutes on a bigger node

# Ticket: orders-api /checkout p99 spikes in the evenings

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Severity | sev3 |
| Service | orders-api, with orders-db |
| First seen | 2026-06-15 19:30 UTC |
| Opened | 2026-06-17 20:40 UTC |
| Closed | 2026-06-18 16:00 UTC |
| Runbooks | RB-020 (checked and ruled out), RB-021 (the lookup investigation) |

**Description.** Evening-only checkout slowness: the tail of `/checkout` jumps past 5 s for a minute or two at a time while the median stays normal. Orders go through; customers sit and wait. The database connection target is `orders-db-01.prod.internal`.

## Comments

**2026-06-16 09:10** · team-commerce, from alert history: on 15 June the checkout p99 alert opened and cleared five times between 19:30 and 22:00, never long enough to page. Same again last night. Put down to evening traffic.

**2026-06-17 20:40** · on-call, team-commerce: paged. Third night of the same shape.

**2026-06-17 20:55** · on-call: gateway logs for `/checkout` show every slow request finishing `200`, with nearly all of its time spent upstream in orders-api. Durations pile up a little past 5 s; a second, smaller pile sits a little past 10 s.

**2026-06-17 21:00** · platform on-call: walked RB-020 in case the database record was flapping in the `prod.internal` zone. `dig` against each internal-dns server gives identical answers and identical serials; coredns journals quiet. Ruled out.

**2026-06-17 21:10** · on-call: orders-api-01, -02 and -03 look healthy by every runtime measure: memory steady, no restarts, the event loop responsive. Something is waiting without blocking.

**2026-06-17 21:25** · on-call: from a pod, resolved the database hostname 200 times with `dns.lookup` and timed each. Nearly all answered within a few milliseconds; two needed a little over five seconds. The delay sits in name resolution.

**2026-06-17 21:40** · on-call: the pod resolver runs with `ndots:5`. Our database hostname contains only two dots, under that threshold, so glibc first tries it with each of the three cluster search suffixes and only then bare, asking for both A and AAAA records each time: 4 × 2 = 8 UDP queries per resolution. When one answer never arrives, the resolver sits out its 5 s timeout and asks again, usually with success. Two dropped answers within one resolution, on different queries, cost about 10 s while the request still succeeds. A query that loses both its attempts ends as `getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN`: five such errors across the three nights, all for a hostname that resolves normally on demand. Why answers get dropped on this cluster is still unknown, and we are not guessing.

**2026-06-17 21:50** · on-call: the burst effect. orders-api's `pg` Pool closes connections idle longer than `idleTimeoutMillis`, left at the 10000 default. Between checkout bursts the pool empties, so each burst reconnects and each reconnect resolves the hostname again. Resolution runs on libuv's 4 worker threads, which file I/O also uses; a couple of resolutions stuck for 5 s leave the rest of the burst queued behind them.

**2026-06-17 22:15** · on-call: nothing safe to change tonight; stays sev3.

**2026-06-18 14:30** · team-commerce: reviewed change. (1) The orders-api Deployment's `dnsConfig` sets `ndots` to "2": the database hostname now goes out unsuffixed first, so one resolution is 2 queries rather than 8, a fourth as many chances to drop an answer. Shorter in-cluster names keep using the suffixes. (2) `idleTimeoutMillis` raised to 60000 so short lulls keep their connections. `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` stays as it is: extra worker threads would mask stalled lookups, not speed them up.

**2026-06-18 15:40** · team-commerce: rollout started.

**2026-06-18 16:00** · team-commerce: rollout complete on all three pods, which now resolve with `ndots:2`. Closing.
resolution: On 18 June orders-api got ndots 2 in its Deployment dnsConfig and the pg Pool idleTimeoutMillis was raised to 60000.
root_cause: Each lookup of orders-db-01.prod.internal under ndots:5 sent 8 UDP queries, and a lost reply cost a 5 s resolver timeout; the pg Pool's 10 s idle timeout made every checkout burst open new connections and repeat the lookup.
symptoms: On three evenings /checkout p99 jumped to about 5 s, with a smaller group near 10 s and a few getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN errors; requests still succeeded.
title: orders-api checkout p99 bursts on three evenings

# Late emails on 29 June 2026 (sev4)

Owner: team-growth. Window: 17:30 to 21:10 UTC. Runbook used: RB-009.

## What customers noticed

On the evening of Monday 29 June, order confirmations and shipping emails arrived late, the worst of them about an hour late. Every email was eventually sent. Nothing else in checkout or payments was involved.

## Timeline (UTC)

- 17:30 · the email provider's API starts answering slowly; consumer lag on `notifications.outbound` begins to climb.
- 17:52 · lag passes 20,000 messages and notification-worker-01 and notification-worker-02 both log `NTF-E710`.
- 18:05 · team-growth on-call picks it up. Both pods healthy, no restarts, sends succeeding, just slowly.
- 18:20 · the provider's status page acknowledges degraded API latency.
- 18:30 · used RB-009's retention check: `notifications.outbound` has no retention override, so it keeps the broker default of 168 h, while lag for the `notification-worker` group was about 54,000 messages. We were minutes behind, not days. No retention change, no disk work.
- 20:30 · the provider recovers; sends are back to their usual speed.
- 20:59 · lag drops below 20,000; `NTF-E710` stops.
- 21:03 · lag reaches zero.
- 21:10 · resolved.

## Why the backlog grew

Each worker pod keeps 20 sends in flight, so the two pods have 40 going at once. At the usual 0.33 s per send that is about 120 sends a second, three times the evening arrival rate of about 40 messages a second. During the slowdown a send took about 1.6 s, so throughput fell to 40 / 1.6 = 25 a second, 15 a second short of what was arriving.

At 15 a second the backlog reached the 20,000 threshold after about 22 minutes, at 17:52. By 18:30 it was 15 × 3,600 = 54,000, which at 40 a second is roughly 23 minutes of mail. By 20:30, three hours in, it stood at about 15 × 10,800 = 162,000, a little over an hour of mail.

Once sends were fast again, the workers ran at about 120 a second against 40 arriving, so the backlog shrank by about 80 a second. Getting from 162,000 down to 20,000 took about 1,775 s, roughly 29 minutes (20:59); emptying it took about 2,025 s (21:03).

## What we did not do

We didn't add pods or raise the in-flight count: the provider was the slow part, and pushing more concurrent requests at a degraded API rarely helps. We didn't touch retention: the oldest unread message was never close to the topic's limit.

## Follow-ups

1. Alert on lag measured in minutes of traffic, not a fixed message count; 20,000 means very different delays at noon and at night.
2. Ask the provider for their incident report.
3. Add a status line to the customer support dashboard when email is running late.
resolution: The provider recovered at 20:30 and the workers drained the backlog by 21:03; nothing was changed on our side.
root_cause: The external email provider's API slowed from about 0.33 s to about 1.6 s per send, cutting notification-worker's throughput below the rate messages arrived.
symptoms: Consumer lag on notifications.outbound climbed for three hours and both notification-worker pods logged NTF-E710; order and shipping emails arrived up to about an hour late.
title: Email provider slowdown left notifications an hour behind

# Two Kafka brokers refused a pushed config

sev2 · 2026-08-13 · 10:12 to 10:36 UTC · cause: kafka · affected: ledger-service, orders-api · runbook: RB-027

| Host or team | UTC | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| kafka-01 | 10:12 | Picked as the canary. The tool replaced `server.properties`, restarted the broker and got exit code 0. A few seconds later the JVM quit with a `ConfigException` naming `message.max.bytes`. |
| whole cluster | 10:13 | Two healthy brokers remained, so each partition kept a second in-sync copy and producers carried on. No page yet: under-replication has to persist ten minutes before anyone is woken. |
| kafka-02 | 10:17 | Its five-minute pause over, the tool repeated the same steps on the next broker, with the same result. |
| producers | 10:17 | One surviving broker cannot provide two in-sync copies (`min.insync.replicas=2`), so every write asking for `acks=all` was rejected. |
| ledger-service | 10:17 | `LEDGER-E455` logged once per ledger entry that could not go out; entries moved to its retry queue and were retried with growing pauses. |
| on-call | 10:19 | Paged for producer failures. |
| on-call | 10:20 | Halted the run. The remaining broker would have been touched at 10:22. |
| kafka-01, kafka-02 | 10:25 | Last known-good `server.properties` pushed back to just these two; brokers started by hand. |
| whole cluster | 10:27 | Both brokers serving; producers succeed again. |
| ledger-service | 10:28 | Retry queue empty. |
| whole cluster | 10:36 | Every partition fully replicated. Closed. |

## Notes

**The bad value.** Kafka parses `message.max.bytes` as an integer count of bytes. Whoever wrote the change wanted roughly ten megabytes and typed `message.max.bytes=10MB`; the parser refuses the suffix and the broker aborts during startup. Ten mebibytes written correctly is 10485760.

**Why the tool saw success.** systemd treats our broker unit as up the instant its process is spawned, so a restart returns 0 even when the JVM is about to abort on its configuration. In August the tool trusted that return code alone, paused for a fixed time and moved on; nothing asked whether a broker had actually rejoined the cluster. Two brokers were gone before a human was involved.

**Effect on each Kafka user.**

| Service | Effect |
|---|---|
| ledger-service | Published nothing for ten minutes and lost nothing. Its retry queue peaked at about 1,200 entries and was empty by 10:28. CPU unchanged. |
| orders-api | Customers could check out the whole time. Order events go to the outbox first; publishing paused, then resumed with a backlog of about 2,400 events and caught up. |
| notification-worker | Idle: with no new messages arriving, it had nothing to fall behind on. |

## Follow-ups

- team-platform: health-check each broker after its push, so a config run halts on the first broker that does not come back.
- Change review: byte-valued Kafka settings must be bare integers; add a lint for unit suffixes.
- On-call note: a halted run is never resumed as-is; the corrected file goes out as a fresh run.
resolution: The run was stopped before the third broker, the previous server.properties was pushed to kafka-01 and kafka-02, and both were started; all replicas were back in sync at 10:36.
root_cause: The rollout tool pushed message.max.bytes=10MB to server.properties; Kafka needs a plain byte count, so each broker refused the file at startup while systemctl restart still exited 0.
symptoms: kafka-01 and kafka-02 exited at startup after a config push; with one broker left, acks=all producers failed and ledger-service queued entries with LEDGER-E455.
title: Pushed Kafka config stopped two brokers
